title: A Study of 139 Cancer Patients Found That Getting Immunotherapy in the Morning Cut Recurrence by 77 Per Cent. The Only Change Was the Clock.
excerpt: Multiple ASCO 2026 presentations and a randomised trial in Nature Medicine now confirm that circadian timing of cancer treatment is not a footnote — it may be one of the most powerful free interventions in oncology.
body:
When Xianghui Zou, an oncology fellow at NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine, presented his data at the American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting on 30 May 2026, the numbers silenced a room that had been sceptical of circadian oncology for years.

In a retrospective study of 139 patients with early-stage triple-negative breast cancer treated at NYU's Perlmutter Cancer Center between July 2021 and June 2025, patients who received their first three immunotherapy infusions before 12:22 pm had a recurrence rate of just 3.7 per cent. Those treated after that time had a recurrence rate of 16.1 per cent — more than four times higher. After adjusting for clinical factors, later immunotherapy timing remained strongly associated with distant recurrence.

The finding was not an outlier.

A Randomised Trial Confirmed It

Earlier this year, Yongchang Zhang of Central South University in Changsha published results from one of the first randomised trials of chronotherapy in Nature Medicine. In patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, those who received chemotherapy and immunotherapy before 3 pm had a 60 per cent reduction in the risk of disease progression compared with those treated after 3 pm. Overall survival showed a 63 per cent lower risk of death in the early-treatment group.

The results held across both squamous and non-squamous subtypes, and across different levels of PD-L1 expression — suggesting the effect is not limited to one biological subgroup.

"Adjusting the infusion time is a simple clinical decision that adds almost no cost," Zhang told New Scientist.

The Biology Is Now Clear

A landmark study published in Cell by researchers at the University of Geneva has identified the mechanism. The team found that tumour-infiltrating CD8+ T cells — the immune cells that checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab rely on — follow a strict circadian rhythm. Their infiltration into tumours peaks at a specific time of day, governed by the rhythmic expression of adhesion molecules on endothelial cells within the tumour.

When the researchers administered CAR T-cell therapy and anti-PD-1 antibodies during peak infiltration times, tumour control improved dramatically in both mouse models and human data. Blocking the circadian gene Bmal1 in endothelial cells disrupted the rhythm and eliminated the timing advantage entirely, confirming that the clock drives the effect.

Sumanta Pal, a medical oncologist at City of Hope who has published his own circadian immunotherapy data, described the randomised evidence as "powerful" and said it "definitely behooves further investigation."

Why This Matters for South Asian Families

South Asians in the United States face disproportionately elevated risks for several cancers, including breast, oral, stomach, and liver cancers. India alone accounts for roughly one in ten of the world's new cancer diagnoses each year, and the Indian diaspora carries many of the same genetic and environmental risk factors.

For the nearly five million Indian Americans navigating the US healthcare system, the implications are practical and immediate. Cancer treatment scheduling is typically assigned based on clinic availability, not biology. Patients rarely question the slot they are given.

The emerging evidence suggests they should.

Pasquale Innominato of the University of Warwick, a leading chronotherapy researcher, said the NYU and Chinese data "further supports the growing number of reports from all over the world describing better results with early time of day of immunotherapy drugs administration."

What Patients Can Do Now

The research is not yet at the level of formal clinical guidelines. No oncology society has issued a recommendation on treatment timing. But the consistency of the data — across retrospective studies in melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, small-cell lung cancer, and now triple-negative breast cancer — has pushed the field past the point of dismissal.

Patients receiving immunotherapy can ask their oncologist whether morning scheduling is available. The intervention costs nothing and carries no additional risk. For a cancer type like triple-negative breast cancer, where recurrence can be devastating and treatment options after relapse are limited, a fourfold difference in recurrence rates demands attention.

"Anything you look at is probably oscillating to one degree or another in your body, and almost every drug you can think of probably would benefit from some time-of-day analysis," Zachary Buchwald, a radiation oncologist at Emory who is leading the TIME trial for timed immunotherapy in skin cancer, told Scientific American.

The clock on your wall may turn out to be the cheapest cancer drug in the building.
